questions.prompt: For $P=(0.40,0.20,0.15,0.15,0.10)$ an optimal Huffman code has lengths $(1,3,3,3,3)$. Compute the expected code length in bits per symbol. (tolerance 0.005)
questions.explanation: **Numeric answer: 2.2** (tolerance 0.005). The expected length is 0.40 · 1 + 0.60 · 3 = 2.20 bits, while the entropy is 2.146 bits. The gap of about 0.054 bits is the price of integer lengths, comfortably inside the guarantee H ≤ L < H + 1.

questions.prompt: Data come from $P=(0.5,0.25,0.25)$ but ideal fractional code lengths are built from the model $Q=(0.25,0.25,0.5)$. Compute the expected length in bits per symbol. (tolerance 0.002)
questions.explanation: **Numeric answer: 1.75** (tolerance 0.002). The expected length is the cross-entropy H₂(P,Q) = 1.75 bits, and the entropy of P is 1.5 bits. The difference of 0.25 bits is D_KL(P‖Q), the mismatch surcharge, before any rounding is considered.

questions.explanation: **Numeric answer: 5.059** (tolerance 0.005). The final interval has width 0.5 · 0.2 · 0.3 = 0.03, so the ideal length is −log₂ 0.03 = 5.059 bits. Terminating the code needs a whole dyadic interval inside the target one, which is why the emitted prefix here is six bits rather than five.

questions.prompt: A Bayesian mixture assigns weight $w_j=1/64$ to model $P_j$. What is the worst-case regret of the mixture relative to $P_j$ on any sequence, in bits? (tolerance 0.005)
questions.explanation: **Numeric answer: 6** (tolerance 0.005). The regret is at most log₂ 64 = 6 bits for the whole sequence, no matter how long it is. Per symbol it therefore tends to zero, which is what makes a mixture a usable universal code.
